Democracy and our voice

Autumn 2 · Week 2 · UK Parliament Week · Whole-school assembly

Democracy and our voice

UK Parliament Week · How decisions are made and how your voice counts.

20 minutes
Think, point, speak or watch.
Nobody is put on the spot.

If a group is choosing a Friday activity, what makes the choice fair?

Discussion / choices: One person decides for everyone · Everyone gets a fair say · Only the loudest person chooses

Key idea: Democracy means people get a fair say in decisions that affect them, rather than just the loudest voice winning.

Presenter: Use the warm-up choice to show that even quiet voices count equally when a vote is fair.

02 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

Decisions affect daily life

1.5–3.5 min

Tap each area to see how public decisions shape life for teenagers.

In a democracy, power does not belong to one person alone.

Decisions in Parliament set funding and rules for schools, exams, and support for young people.
Laws and budgets shape transport, road safety, and how local neighbourhoods are looked after.
Public choices decide how health care, leisure spaces, and community support are run.

Discussion / choices: Schools, training, and youth services · Buses, roads, and safe public spaces · Hospitals, sport, and local parks

Key idea: Public decisions shape everyday life, so everyone needs fair ways to be represented and heard.

Presenter: Tap each card and connect it to everyday places pupils recognise.

03 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

How representatives check a plan

3.5–6 min

Watch the scene. Pause at the prediction point and decide what representatives should check.

Parliament checks ideas before they become rules for everyone.

Young people and residents explain that a busy road outside school needs a safer crossing. Pause here: before making a rule or spending public money, what should representatives check? Representatives question the plan, suggest improvements, and vote on the clearest option. Fair rules work better when people have been heard and the reasons are clear.

PAUSE · PREDICT · REPLAY

Prediction point — why check different views instead of rushing straight to a decision?

Captioned · works offline without internet · optional local video slot

Scene summary / still alternative
  1. A local issue is raised: Young people and residents explain that a busy road outside school needs a safer crossing.
  2. Checking different views and costs: Pause here: before making a rule or spending public money, what should representatives check?
  3. Debate, changes, and a fair vote: Representatives question the plan, suggest improvements, and vote on the clearest option.
  4. Putting the decision into action: Fair rules work better when people have been heard and the reasons are clear.

Discussion / choices: Watch the scene. Pause at the prediction point and decide what representatives should check.

Key idea: Checking evidence and hearing different views helps spot problems early and makes the final decision fairer.

Presenter: Play the offline animation and pause at the prediction point. Ask what could go wrong if nobody checked the plan first.

04 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

What is a representative's job?

6–8 min

Voters in each area choose a Member of Parliament (MP). Tap each duty to see how they work.

A representative speaks up for people in their local area, even those who did not vote for them.

Discussion / choices: Listen to local people's concerns · Ask questions and check the government · Debate and vote on proposed laws

Key idea: Representatives listen to local people, question people in power, and vote on laws.

Presenter: Compare an MP representing a local area with a school council rep bringing tutor group ideas to staff.

05 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

How a bill becomes a law

8–10 min

Tap the four steps in the order a new law travels through Parliament.

A proposed law is called a bill until every step is complete.

Discussion / choices: ROYAL ASSENT (LAW) · DEBATE & AMENDMENT · PROPOSAL (BILL) · TWO CHAMBERS VOTE

Key idea: PROPOSAL (BILL) → DEBATE & AMENDMENT → TWO CHAMBERS VOTE → ROYAL ASSENT (LAW).

Presenter: Walk through the four steps: an idea starts as a bill, gets debated and amended, is voted on by both chambers, and receives formal approval.

06 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

Disagreeing with respect

10–12 min

Sort each comment: is it respectful debate or an unfair personal attack?

Strong debate focuses on the problem and the evidence, not insulting the person.

Discussion / choices: Sort each comment: is it respectful debate or an unfair personal attack?

Key idea: Respectful debate challenges the idea with reasons and listens to other views.

Presenter: Read each card aloud and take a hall point or thumb vote before tapping the category.

07 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

Why we use a secret ballot

12–14 min

Tap the three highlighted parts to see what keeps a vote fair.

Fair rules protect everyone, even people whose choice did not win the vote.

In a fair election, every voter gets an cast in , and the are still protected.

EQUAL: One person's vote counts the same as anyone else's.

PRIVATE: A secret ballot means nobody can pressure or bully you over how you voted.

PROTECTED: Winning a majority vote never gives anyone the right to mistreat a smaller group.

Discussion / choices: equal vote · private · rights of everyone

Key idea: An equal vote, a private ballot, and protection for everyone's rights keep democracy fair.

Presenter: Explain why voting in private stops peer pressure and keeps choices honest.

08 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

Practising a fair choice

14–16.5 min

If our group had 20 minutes of extra Friday time, which option would you choose?

Point, show 1, 2 or 3 on fingers, or watch.

Discussion / choices: Quiet reading, drawing, or music space · Sports court or outdoor games · Practical workshop, crafts, or board games

Key idea: People have different preferences. A fair decision hears every option and looks for ways everyone is included.

Presenter: Tap whichever option the group points to first, then tap the other two to show why all three views make sense.

09 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

Using your voice in school

16.5–18.5 min

You do not have to wait until adulthood to use your voice. Tap each step for raising an idea.

Not every request can be granted, but a clear reason helps your idea be heard.

Describe the practical issue calmly rather than blaming individuals.
Explain why it matters for safety, learning, or fairness.
Use tutor feedback, school council, a written note, or a conversation with staff to share the suggestion.

Discussion / choices: 1. Name what is happening clearly · 2. Explain how it affects people · 3. Suggest a realistic step to try

Key idea: Clear facts, a fair reason, and a practical suggestion help pupil voice make a real difference.

Presenter: Remind pupils of the routes available in school, including written notes or support cards for anyone who prefers not to speak aloud.

10 / 10 · Autumn 2 · Week 2 · British values · Democracy

What makes pupil voice strong?

18.5–20 min

Choose the two ideas that help a suggestion get heard.

Think it through before the reveal.

Discussion / choices: Explain the problem and suggest a fair solution · Shout over other people so they cannot speak · Listen to how the change affects everyone

Key idea: Explaining a fair solution and listening to others are the heart of democracy in school and in society.

Presenter: Close by thanking pupils for sharing their views respectfully.

Word help

democracy
A system where people have a say in how their community or country is run.
representative
Someone chosen by voters to speak, question, and vote on behalf of a group.
bill
A written proposal for a new law, or a plan to change an existing law.
amendment
A change made to improve a bill after people debate and check the details.
royal assent
The final formal approval that turns an agreed bill into an Act of Parliament.
majority
More than half of the votes cast in a decision.

Teacher desk

20-minute assembly · secondary SEMH

Participation and delivery

Read every prompt and option aloud. Pupils may answer by pointing, thumbs, speaking, or simply watching. Staff operate the board; nobody needs to type. Allow processing time. Do not require eye contact or invite personal disclosures.

Keep political institutions factual and impartial. Connect national democracy to everyday fairness, listening, and pupil voice in school. Never require a pupil to speak in front of the hall.
